utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Brdjanin. General Talic, good morning to you too. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General Talic. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Anna Richterova and Julian Nicholls for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, madam. Appearance for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm with my co-counsel, Milan Trbojevic, and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Ackerman. And appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as we closed yesterday I told you I wanted the evening to think about some proposals I want to make to you regarding the Witness 52. Your Honours will remember that on Monday I brought to your attention my concern about the apparently closed-ended time that he was scheduled to be here and suggested that once a witness is here that it should be up to Your Honours how long they are here and not the witness himself. We were then told yesterday that the witness must leave and not be here after Tuesday, and therefore we all have to change our lives to accommodate his business interests. And I don't think that is an appropriate situation for us to find ourselves in. On Monday we were handed two fairly large packets of material. Because of other responsibilities regarding this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. Could the usher please inform the witness that once more we have a procedural problem that we are dealing with and that is why we are keeping him waiting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We were both -- both teams were handed fairly large packets of materials. Because of other responsibilities, I was not able to begin looking at those materials until Wednesday, at which point I discovered that there were two -- three additional transcripts of prior testimony of Witness 52 contained in those materials. On Thursday, when I arrived here, I spoke with Ms. Gustin regarding the B/C/S versions of those transcripts and whether the tapes were ready for our clients to listen to or not, and I was told that they were not ready and she didn't know exactly when they would be ready. But the bottom line is that Mr. Brdjanin has not had an opportunity to listen to the tapes of those three transcripts that were provided to us on Monday. Now, Your Honour, those transcripts are from testimony of 13 and 14 May 1999. I cannot imagine how under the -- any conditions at all there's any excuse for waiting until Monday of this week to supply us with those materials and to not have prepared the tapes in B/C/S for our clients. This should have been done before this case started because this witness was known to the Prosecutor and known that this witness was going to be brought here before this case started. So in view of that, I am not of a mind to be very accommodating regarding Ms. Korner's requests of yesterday. I will make to you this proposal, which might solve the problem and might accommodate everyone's needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. Let him testify on direct in this Chamber tomorrow and then let the Stakic case have him until -- through Monday and then bring him back here on Tuesday for cross-examination. That is based upon the proposition that the Prosecutor can supply us the tapes that I can get to Mr. Brdjanin by today or tomorrow so I can take instructions from him regarding this. Now, Ms. Korner or the Prosecutor will tell you that there is nothing in these transcripts or the tapes that's relevant to anything that they're going to ask this witness. But very frankly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What she said yesterday - sorry to interrupt you - was that the events that Mr. McLeod testified upon on those two previous occasions were not in any way related to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- now, whatever. I'm not in a position to confirm or deny that because obviously I have never gone to -- I don't even have the transcripts that you have been given. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. And it may very well be the case that once we get through this material, we'll take that same position, but I can't have Ms. Korner deciding what's relevant for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My client needs to hear this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither you nor the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And my proposal would be that, that we have him here on direct tomorrow, that once he's finished his direct that he goes on to the Stakic case or whatever they want to do with him, that he's back here Tuesday for cross-examination. I think that might solve everybody's problem. If it doesn't, then he can come back, you know, when the Prosecution can get him back here, but I don't think we should be forced into a cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before I -- before we pass on your suggestion to Ms. Richterova for onward -- or onward transmission to Ms. Korner, Mr. Zecevic, would you agree with the suggestion that Mr. Ackerman is putting forward?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We do join with the submission of Mr. John Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Ms. Gustin or Ms. Richterova or Mr. Nicholls - I don't know who will be the ambassador amongst you in this particular case - could you convey the suggestion made by Mr. Ackerman and endorsed by Mr. Zecevic to Ms. Korner and -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will convey these messages. I think it's possible to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In which case, then, you have -- you will need to do two things -- or, rather, three things. First thing, make sure that the first of the other two witnesses, that is 7.135, if I remember well. I may be mistaken in the number, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, 139. Will give evidence today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would wish -- I would wish that I manage to finish both these witnesses, because they are talking only about one incident, and I want to focus only, and only on that incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's not waste time talking and discussing that. Please convey the suggestion made by Mr. -- by the two Defence teams to Ms. Korner, and if we could have feedback by the first break, I think that would be extremely useful. Next thing I would like you to convey to Ms. Korner, next message, is this: We would like -- we were discussing amongst ourselves, and we would like to be in a position to have a schedule in place right through the end of December. And our suggestion to both sides is to sit together as you did previously and then submit to the Chamber what your preferences would be for breaks, in other words. The only thing that we might come up with is that there may be a couple of dates that we ourselves would require but shouldn't -- I don't think that's going to make any big difference. So please do sit down. If you could come back to us by either Monday or early next week, then we could have the timetable, the time schedule -- the time schedule in place and so that you would know where you stand between now and December. Yes, Mr. Cayley. I see that you must have been watching --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I was actually walking out of the building and I heard Mr. Ackerman's dulcet tones, and I was listening to what he was saying, and I just wanted to clarify with the Court about these two transcripts, because I was actually involved in one of the two other cases, and they actually have absolutely nothing to do with this case. They're actually concerning another conflict in Bosnia, the Muslim-Croat conflict. And whereas in principle Mr. Ackerman is absolutely right, he should have these materials available to him. I don't think in any way he is going to be prejudiced -- his client is going to be prejudiced by not having the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, he did not bring up the matter as a casus belli in order to start an argument, because all in all -- I mean, he just made his point but then also made a practical suggestion. So let's concentrate on the practical suggestion and leave the rest, because -- I mean, let's not argue about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to make it clear to the Court that these transcripts are not a problem. And in terms of the practical suggestion, I actually think it's probably quite a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So two feedbacks. One today and one as soon as practicable. The one today is whether we are taking up Mr. Ackerman's suggestion regarding Witness 7.52, McLeod. And second feedback coming next week: How do you intend to have -- or what are your preferences for a time schedule for this case between first -- end of August, when we resume, until the end of September [sic] when we go into recess, end of September [sic] when we go into recess in September [sic] anyway. In December, sorry. In December. Okay. Like we did previously. In other words, when you -- beforehand when we were going to have breaks and when we are sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was thinking about the same thing myself this week. The thing that kept me from starting that on my own was that we don't know when we're returning from the August break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you my intention is to start working again the last week of August, because the official break terminates, I think, on the 23rd of August, if I remember well. I'm speaking from memory. The official break of the Tribunal finishes 23rd of August. And my intention was to start on the 26th, if I remember well, which is a Monday, the 26th of August. That would give us the last week of August as the first week after the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then the other thing that I don't know is when the December break begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The December break -- I think there is a plenary in -- 11th, 12th, something like that, and after that you have the break. More or less I think -- I am on duty starting from the 13th to the 20th of December, so I'll still be enjoying the beautiful weather of The Hague, but I think we would have already started the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But in the meantime, I can have that checked. Ms. Registrar, you can check exactly when the -- there is a document which I have already, which was circulated in the beginning of the year -- so that we can give the information. The witness. You can bring him in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good morning to you, Mr. Biscevic, hoping that this will be your last day in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you Mr. Biscevic, hoping that this will be your last day in this Tribunal. Once more please proceed with making the -- entering the same solemn declaration as before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You my sit down. Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday before we adjourned we were speaking about the 20th of April. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1992. Could you tell me, after that incident in Sanski Most there weren't any other large-scale incidents until the 25th of May; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, the situation in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina had dramatically -- or was dramatically deteriorating from the 20th of April to the 25th of May, during that period.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was arrested, and on the 3rd of May, a column in Sarajevo was attacked in Dobrovoljacka Street a column was attacked. 160 and 200 people were wounded in an ambush. You know about all these things, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Biscevic, you said that on the 27th of May you were arrested and then taken to the area of the village of Magarice; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Before the 27th of May, you were in that village Magarice or not -- were you in that village or not?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, on the 27th of May, you were taken there -- he took you there and he showed you the town and he said, "Look, can you see what you did?"

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal in 1997 and 1999, you said that at the time he was thinking of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he told that to me he was thinking of the party in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that same statement, on page 00838010 you said in your statement of 1997 and 1999, you said the following. I'll read it out in English and it will be translated to you. [In English] "Major Vukic was Basara's deputy. He had come from Tuzla where he used to serve as an active-duty JNA officer. Vukic told me that he had come from Tuzla when he interrogated me after my arrest. He was born in the village of Dabar in the vicinity of Sanski Most and that is why Vukic came to Sanski Most. He had to leave Tuzla after the Bosnians forced the JNA to leave Tuzla." [Interpretation] Do you remember giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you stand by what you said?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The major told you this on that occasion, on the 27th of May, or did he tell you something before that date, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the time we were in that curing hut, and then he told me, "I'm from Tuzla. I've been expelled. I've come to Sanski Most." Whether it's Branko Vukic, I don't know. But from those two villages somewhere in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, yesterday you told us that at some time there was -- there were groups of paramilitary formations of the army.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the Serbian people were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that members of other nationalities were armed?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't armed in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So when you say that "they weren't armed," you want to say that they weren't armed in Sanski Most, in the Sanska Valley, in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a paramilitary formation called the SOS? We mentioned them yesterday.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've heard about this formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That was also a paramilitary formation.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it was. I know that it was the Patriotic League, that this was established. But what happened to that Patriotic League, what it did, I don't know. But I know that it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Patriotic League was a military formation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was formed in Sarajevo. I don't know whether it was a military or civil organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether on the 11th of June, 1992 a great meeting of the headquarters of the Patriotic League was held in Dosici Nikolecija [phoen], and it was attended by presidents of the municipalities and municipal organisations of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The people who belonged, such private army formations, paramilitary formations, or groups of armed men, they didn't participate -- they weren't included in any official military or police units, were they?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a legal army which had been issued weapons and uniforms, and later it was part of a particular party, the SDS or the SOS or the command of the 6th Corps. These were all armed formations and they had various branches and belonged to certain parties. But they were all armed and they had illegally been issued weapons. They had received these weapons legally from the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me -- could you tell me how you know this?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was common practice in the last -- in the most recent days, the helicopters come from the Banja Luka area. They would land in Serbian villages, and they would distribute weapons. And a second -- well, it wasn't a secret but it was something that was publicly known. Mico Krunic was given a bus. He took the windows out and covered them with tin sheets and took weapons to villages, Serbian villages, and distributed these people to the Serbian villages on a daily basis. My son had a girlfriend in a village, in a settlement, in our settlement where the majority of the population that was Serbian. They received flats which they -- in which they lived. The mother of his girlfriend said -- her neighbour said that on that night, every Serbian flat had to put a window in the -- a candle in the window, and that was a sign that the house was a Serbian one, and then they would distribute weapons. We didn't believe that because that was a little earlier on. But later on, it proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly -- if I have understood you correctly, what you have just told us, you saw none of this personally. You heard about this.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mico Krunic. I was watching every day, and I could see the helicopters every day with my own eyes. I wasn't there when helicopters arrived in the Serbian village and distributed weapons, but I saw the helicopter-- helicopters, and I knew why it had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, around that time many people put on uniforms for no particular reason?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had a uniform, maybe they put it on. It wasn't necessary, because they had uniforms which had been legally issued to them. So they could put them on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you said, in your statement of 1995 which you gave in the court in Sanski Most, you said that Vlado Vrkes, the President of the SDS, had been going there recently. I think you're referring to the period before the 25th of May. You said that he would come to the meetings in the municipality wearing a uniform and carrying a weapon. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came to our meetings in uniform and he had a revolver. We laughed at him and joked about it with him. We didn't think it was anything in particular, but he was very official. He said, "This is the weapon I have been issued with, and I carry it with me quite legally throughout the day and throughout the town." And it wasn't just Vlado Vrkes but other leaders at the time. They had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us yesterday that Rajkica Stanic, a Judge from Sanski Most, had put on a uniform and acted as some sort of a coordinator, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't act as a coordinator. He was literate. He was an attorney, and he worked as a civilian in the court in Sanski Most. When the war came, in my opinion all those people working in MUP were not of the same profession. They were not qualified. So he would come and go and talk to the interrogator. He wasn't acting or pretending to be a coordinator but he was the coordinator because of his qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, before April and May 1992, there were no stationary garrison of the JNA in Sanski Most, was there?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When on the 27th of May you were taken to the village of Magarice or the area of the village of Magarice, as far as you know, was there any kind of a permanent military facility there, a warehouse or something like that, before that, before the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing permanent there before or after that, but the 6th Corps came. They took the weapons into the meadow. There were boxes of weapons piled up, and there were mortars and there was a provisional canteen, and the soldiers were sleeping in the stables or around there. There was nothing organised. It wasn't prepared in advance. It was as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So we will agree that this was a kind of provisional camp?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, provisional.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday -- I'm sorry, the day before yesterday, that you were taken that same day to the radio station where you read out a statement that had been prepared and which we heard the day before played in this courtroom. Isn't at that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I should like to read to you a part of that statement of yours if you remember. We heard it the day before yesterday. On page 10 of the Serbian version of the transcript -- of the statement, or page 6 of the English version, the last three sentences which in English begins, "That is why we are prepared...." I'm going to read it to you in Serbian. "That is why we are prepared, on the orders of the Serb armed forces, to come out before our people and to be judged by our people in the next few days. I assure you that the command of the Serbian armed forces which is carrying out the armed activities in Sanski Most was forced into such behaviour by our lies and sycophancy." End of quote. Do you remember reading that out on that occasion in Sanski Most, in Radio Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what I read, but I heard it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You heard it yesterday on a tape?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard my voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, for the needs of this Court and people who don't speak our language, the abbreviation for "Serbian armed forces" is SOS, is it not, S-O-S?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as far as you know, this statement that you read in Radio Sanski Most on that day, did it have any effect in the sense that you had made a call for weapons to be surrendered? Did it have any effect at all, if you know?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but the JNA knew exactly what they were doing. They knew that I was very influential in Sanski Most, that I come from a wealthy, noble family, a dentist, a jeweller in Sanski Most, highly influential. And the Muslims and Croats, some of them at least, believed what they heard, and those that hadn't surrendered their weapons until then did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, after this did you go to the Radio Sanski Most on any other occasion to read statements, different statements? Do you remember that, any other statement?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The major, whatever his name was, Brajic or Vukic, in Magarice spoke to me. Now, whether he taped that or not, I don't know, but I didn't go to the radio station again. But I did hear myself, in prison, speaking on Radio Sana, and then I realised that everything had been taped and that they aired it even though I was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, your conversation with this major or some other person was taped and, after that, broadcast.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Probably. If there was any other statement, then it was probably taped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read out to you from the same transcript of the audiotape that we heard the day before yesterday on page 01907762 of the English version and the B/C/S version, 01104887. This is P827 A. And it says the following: "Male voice: Muslims and Croats to hand over their legal and illegal weapons to the Serbian authorities, not to fall prey to Muslim or Croat extremists, nor to the tale they tell, because that would lead to the large-scale suffering of innocent people. We have now shown who and what we are, accusing and blaming one another. Our people have seen through us and don't trust us any longer. That is why I ask you to respond to the legitimate Serbian army and authorities. The Serbian army has already made a few announcements and has given us the opportunity to surrender, so please heed the appeal and hand over your weapons to the commander of the Serbian army, where I have been staying for two days now and I am personally convinced that it is the most humane army I have ever met," et cetera. The last sentence: "Announcement written by Faik Biscevic." Mr. Biscevic, do you remember writing a proclamation of this kind?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, so you don't know whether your statement produced any result, or rather, both of these statements, all these statements, whether it had any effect in terms of the surrender of weapons by Muslims and Croats, do you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know, when I was in prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mean did you learn later after being released from prison? Did anyone tell you about it, that they heeded what you said in your announcement on the radio, if you know?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know very well. They didn't need to heed anyone. The practice of the Yugoslav People's Army was to go to Muslim and Croat villages and their streets and to collect or round up the population, to separate men to one side, women to another. And anyone found after that would be executed, because on that first day 43 civilians were killed in Sanski Most who were in hospitals and their apartments. They were collected on the third day and buried in a mass grave at the cemetery in Sanski Most. Therefore, my statement had the least effect on them because they had no chance of surrendering anything. They simply had to. They were simply rounded up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, I asked you in connection with weapons. My question was related to weapons. So could you please answer that for me. You've already explained this whole procedure. I was just asking you about the weapons. Did your statement have any effect on the Muslims and Croats to surrender their weapons, if you know?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you. I was in prison, so how could I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My colleague is telling me that all that you said a moment ago also happened while you were in prison, yet you are aware of it, whereas you are not aware of what I am asking you about.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Would you rephrase it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you just in a minute. You spoke about the practice of the Yugoslav People's Army, and this was in response to my question about weapons. You spoke about the practice of the Yugoslav People's Army and said that on that first day, 43 civilians were killed in Sanski Most, that they were rounded up on the third day and -- sorry, collected and buried in a mass grave at the cemetery in Sanski Most. So my question is: Since at that point in time you were under arrest, you were in detention, you were in prison when all this was going on, so how is it you know about this?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my release.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Biscevic. After spending some 30 hours with the army, as you told us, you were transferred to the MUP building in Sanski Most. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you spent 95 days there, until the 27th of August, 1992 when the police transferred you to Manjaca and handed you over to them there.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, during this period of detention in Sanski Most, you were guarded by members of the police, were you not?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 1997 and 1999 you said that they wore police uniforms and that Bosko Kuzmanovic, an active policeman, was their commander. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosko Kuzmanovic was one of the shift leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The police was escorting all people to Manjaca, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were transported by vehicles and escorted by the police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your particular case, on the 27th of August when you reached Manjaca, it was only at the entrance to Manjaca that the police handed you over to the officers of Republika Srpska; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official police had no access to the Manjaca camp, the complex; only outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, so this was happening at the very entrance to the camp, at the fence.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you were handed over to the officers and soldiers of Republika Srpska under their competence; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The bus went as far as the gate on the outside. It stopped. We got off, lined up four by four, and waited to enter. And as soon as we entered, the police had nothing more to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me please, on the 15th of November, when you were released, the situation was the same, wasn't it? The procedure was the same.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mean that the Army of Republika Srpska went as far as the fence --

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When we were released, 12 buses came. I was in the fourth or fifth. A representative of the International Community was with us on the bus. And the escort, the security of the buses -- I didn't pay attention. I don't know who provided the escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to the time you spent in Sanski Most. During your detention in Sanski Most, that was in the remand custody. You were held in remand custody, were you not?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you know that as a professional. We know that we had special treatment. We were under lock and key. The shift leader was responsible for us and he was the only one allowed to unlock and lock the gates, according to the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So let me rephrase the question, make myself clearer. Do you know that the purpose of the premises in which you were kept from the, shall I say, the 29th of May until the 27th of August, 1992 in Sanski Most - even before May 1992 - was as an investigating prison or detention on remand? That is what it was used for. I am talking about the building.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you call it. We know that it was the city prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A municipal prison in your view implies a prison attached to the police station in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the conditions that you found there in that prison, the city prison, as you call it, in May 1992 were the same even before 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was just asking you whether you know.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your time in those cells, other persons were brought there, the perpetrators of some criminal acts; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were coming, others going, on a daily basis almost. So what was going on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday in transcript page 22, line 10 to 13 that on one occasion a Serb soldier had been brought in who activated a hand grenade who was afterwards beaten for as long as he could speak. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Also yesterday, on the unofficial transcript, on page 19, lines 11 to 15, you explained that running water in that building of the city prison in Sanski Most did not exist because of lack of electricity, and the fact that the water supply system worked in such a way that the pumps pumped the water up to higher levels and these provided the city with water. Tell me, please, this system, water supply system, was the water supply system, wasn't it? The whole town was provided with water in the same way?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which means that no citizens of Sanski Most could have water when there was no electricity. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, no one could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, yesterday while you were testifying in answer to a question from the Prosecution, you described in detail the appearance of the room in which you were held, and among other things, you said that there was sheet steel on the window with small holes drilled into it of four millimetres each, so that there wasn't enough air in the room. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about four millimetres but exactly four millimetres. And those holes were made by Redzo Kurbegovic, as he was an expert. And he did this before the war. And we joked with him and said, "How could you have made such tiny holes?" So it is true. There was a sheet steel cover, and the holes drilled in it were of four millimetres diameter. Yes, it was fixed so that the room was hermetically closed, probably to prevent anyone from escaping. But it was placed there, as we heard, just in case anyone would want to throw in a hand grenade. So the sheet steel was fixed very firmly, and there was no air as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You say that this was hermetically --

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was nailed in, nailed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So light, sound could hardly penetrate those tiny holes.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As this window was to the east, in the morning there would be some light. And after 11.00 it was semi-darkness. And in the afternoon, it was total darkness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was it also difficult to hear anything?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no glass, and one could hear much better than if there were glass panes. The doors were metal, so one could hear through that too. And people spoke in a normal loud voice. There was no need to whisper, so that things could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you all this because yesterday, at one point in time you said that as far as you knew, soldiers, upon returning from the front, were lined up on a plateau close to the city prison where you were being detained. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a plateau but a soccer field that was separated from the prison by a wall. There was a football pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know, then, that they were lined up on this football field? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard the officers making speeches, distributing decorations, appraising certain combatants, whether they would cheer. When Lieutenant Colonel Basara would say something then they would cheer. Then there would be shooting. There was just a wall separating the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you saw this or not.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you nicely. We heard it. We couldn't see when it was not possible to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, sir, while you were in this investigating prison, you told us that you were questioned about supplies of weapons for the SDA, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Questions also had to do with collecting funds for the purchase of weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no question about money.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned, if I remember correctly, that the investigator, Mima Dosenovic in those days, asked you in connection with some debt that you had to another fellow citizen of yours. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alagic, photographer, is my neighbour, and I borrowed some money from him which I didn't pay back for a certain period of time. He said this in a restaurant, and an informer heard this and told Mima. And then he said, "You see, you had money for weapons." But this money was something I needed to do a general service for my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My question was precisely whether Mima Dosenovic had asked but the collection of money for weapons. Your answer was no, so I've just reminded you. So he did ask you about collecting funds for weapons, because he thought that the money you had borrowed from your fellow citizen was allegedly being used for the purchase of weapons; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He specifically mentioned Riza Alagic because he knew exactly who the money had been borrowed from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me Mr. Biscevic, please, whether you really did procure weapons for the SDA or not.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you procured weapons for the Party of Democratic Action in Sanski Most. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you told us that when this statement was being taken from you that you were first beaten by the investigator Mima Dosenovic, who was a policeman, and another person who kept -- who wrote the record, and then two men in uniform whom you didn't know and who came with this Rajkica Stanisic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't come with Rajkica, but they came in when Mima came out. And Rajko came when Mima was there, and he would talk to Mima. He didn't beat people, he just talked to Mima. He didn't talk to me and he just went off. And the soldiers came in after Mima left. They didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, these two persons who were wearing military uniforms and whom you didn't know, do you remember what kind of uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all wore those camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "everyone," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniforms of the Serbian army. As they were wearing shirts, they had short-sleeved shirts. It was summertime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about these two men. What sort of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two men too, camouflage uniforms, military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did they have some sort of insignia on those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had some sort of mark here and they had some sort of tags. Whether they had them at the moment -- whether those two men had them, I don't know. I wasn't looking. But all soldiers had some sort of insignia, yellow, green, white insignia. What it was exactly, I don't know, but they had this on the soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "tag," do you mean bands of some kind?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A sort of band which is tied here. A sort of braid. And it would be tied here on the epaulettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In different countries --

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't sewed in. It would be tied -- tied up, perhaps so that it would be possible to change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, we'll finish this very rapidly now. Tell me, you were taken to Manjaca on the 27th of August, 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in the former JNA? Did you serve in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where and when?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Ljubljana and in Sarajevo. I was a part of the medical corps. I was a reserve officer in the medical corps when I finished -- towards the end of my service in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what year that was.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1963. That's when I was a Second Lieutenant in the medical corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As a reserve officer in the medical corps, you are surely aware of the procedure for bringing recruits to do their military service.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They go for a medical check-up, they're registered, and then they are given accommodation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that is a very similar to the procedure through which you went when on the 27th of August, 1992 you arrived in Manjaca. I am referring to the medical check-up, being registered and being provided with -- being provided with accommodation.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not at all the same. How could it be the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, from Manjaca -- you were released on the 15th of November, 1992 from Manjaca; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave here, you mentioned a certain boy who was underage, someone from your town - I assume that was Sanski Most - and you said that he was a retarded boy and his name was Senad Kalic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: According to the list that we have, the person with that name was pardoned by decision of the main headquarters of the Republika Srpska and he was released on the same day as you, on the 14th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the only thing that doesn't agree with this is that according to the list, Senad Kalic was born in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1962. Correction.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I want to mean that in 1992 he was 30 years old. He wasn't underage. He wasn't a minor.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. That confirms what I said, because my father was over 50 and they had no other solution other than to send him with his -- send him away with his father. That was the only solution. They didn't know what they would do with him without his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you allow for the possibility that this boy was not a minor. You said he was retarded. I'm only asking you whether it is possible that the boy in question was not a minor, since on the basis of the documents that we have that person, who has that name from Sanski Most, he was born in 1962, which means that in August 1992 he was about 30 years old.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are playing with words. It is a custom among us to say that a retarded person is -- has a child's mind. But although he was 30 years old, they released him as if he were a child of ten years old. For what were they to do with him, because he was less than a minor. That is probably why he was released. It was an exception of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have solved that. Obviously they didn't understand you, because in the -- in the transcript it said "a minor." It didn't say "someone who was retarded." Thank you, Mr. Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First, I didn't want to interrupt the cross-examination, but for the record could he -- could counsel state what list he was referring to, what document he was reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to know what he means by "this list of names we have."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a list of names. It's something that we verified. Our investigators verified this. And according to the name that the witness gave to us, we've verified the facts relating to this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I would like to see the list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But she's telling you there was no list -- she verified -- the mentioning of a list was obviously a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Mr. Biscevic, you're now going to be cross-examined by Mr. Trbojevic, who is co-counsel for Mr. Brdjanin. Thank you. And again, same recommendation, allow a pause, because Mr. Trbojevic has exactly the same problem that Mr. Zecevic has. Thank you. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's okay. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Biscevic, you said that were -- are a politician, a political leader.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after the multi-party elections, together with the SDS and HDZ you formed a coalition government in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: If we assume that at one of those many meetings that you had on the agenda was the formation of these authorities. That's -- would that be a correct assumption?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1991, those authorities started functioning.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1991, there were political differences among these parties.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you didn't go into details, you didn't explain this in detail, you didn't explain these differences in detail.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it -- would it have been necessary to explain anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you would agree with me that one of the main differences was the fact that the political position of the SDA was that Bosnia and Herzegovina should separate from Yugoslavia, and the SDS's position was that it should remain within Yugoslavia, that Bosnia and Herzegovina should remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: These were the themes of the referendum, of the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And this resulted in absolutely and totally contradictory positions -- contrary positions on the part of these parties.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't so much an obstacle. It wasn't so prominent at the time. But it became prominent later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: After the 6th of April, when the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been declared, it was practically no longer possible to work together, to follow a common direction.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We nevertheless discussed matters in Sanski Most and we would meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right to say that at the time talks about a possible division of the territory commenced, of the division of institutions, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were discussions, but towards the end in May, when everything had collapsed, then people started talking about dividing the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And these discussions finished with that situation when the police force was divided. The Serbian police remained in the police building and the Muslim force in the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the police station was taken over, then the Serbian Sanski Most was declared. And when the municipality building was attacked, then all ties were severed, and that's when it finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the war events in Slovenia and Croatia, which happened a little before the events we are talking about, would you agree that these affected, in an important manner, the events in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the fact that some of the police were mobilised and there weren't as many who were within the police force. I'm referring to the return of armed reservists with their weapons. And I'm also thinking of the decision on the part of the SDA that Muslims should no longer go and join the JNA.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that the cause of that decision by the Party of Democratic Action not to join the JNA any longer, the cause of this decision was the fact that there were Muslim soldiers who had been killed, who had been killed by being shot in the back.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Don't you think that the political position of the SDA was more important, more important than certain individual cases if such cases had occurred?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. As far as the individuals are concerned, those who returned and who were killed, we couldn't do much about that. That was a matter for the army. But our position was that if anyone had to go from Sanski Most, they should remain in Sanski Most, not go to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But that decision was taken in Sarajevo, wasn't it, without the -- without the presence of the Serbian members?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina without the Serbian members.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to return to the beginning. On page 2 of the statement that you gave to the investigators of the Prosecution, when you spoke about important people, people who were important for the situation, you started with Rasula, and you said that you went to school together, et cetera. You said he was a -- he was a pro-Serb. What were you referring to exactly when you side that he was a pro-Serb and that he was in favour of the Serbian cause?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The monument to his father -- on the monument to his father, he said, "My father was killed by state enemies." You can see that to this very day. It hasn't been destroyed. Whenever anything had to happen, was to happen between the Muslims and the Serbs, he would be the one in charge. When he graduated in Sanski Most, Avdo Umcanin was the director of the secondary school. And as soon as he came with his brother Sofia and Slobodan - I don't know what the name is - they just replaced Avdo, retired him summarily, and then Rasula became the director because he thought the director of a secondary school had to be a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Rasula sought -- provided the Serbs who had graduated with important positions.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was common practice then. It wasn't common practice then, but always later on most personnel would come from the village. And in the town we also had graduated professionals but these professionals weren't able to take up important posts. The custom in our place was that if you wanted to be a politician, you should finish political school and then you would become an official because that was a condition to hold such a post.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. There's a certain lack of tolerance on the local level between the town and the village.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More or less that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But if on page 4 of this same statement you told us that before the war the police in Sanski Most was about -- 90 [Realtime transcript read in error "09"] per cent of the police was Serb and the leader was Salko Coric. Doesn't that indicate that the leading positions were important and occupied by Muslims too, even in such a situation where a large number -- we say that if someone had -- it was just for show, to show people that it was mixed up. Salko Coric was a communist, and a condition for him to hold that post was for him to be a communist. So that means that he had severed ties with Muslims, with religion, et cetera. Then he would assume such a post. And this was just for show.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the -- those were the policies at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, in the beginning of your question the transcript says "09 per cent of the police were Serb." In actual fact, I heard the interpretation say "90 per cent." Just for the record. It's corrected then later on, but I think for the record we need to clarify it. Thank you. You may proceed Mr. Trbojevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown P832 , Exhibit P832.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's a record of the release of your son from Manjaca, and you have had it in your hands already. It says: "Record on the release of someone from Manjaca, of the release of a person from the Manjaca Prisoners of War Camp." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the following sentence?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the basis of an order from Colonel Stevo Bogojevic, Biscevic Nedim, son of Faik, is being released from the Sanski Most camp."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can remove that. There is nothing of interest for me in this document any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: From the very first day, we spoke about the notes that you had before you. You told us that you had made notes, so I assume -- so you will be able to give a fuller and more detailed testimony here. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And if I suggested that you should provide us with these notes and provide the Trial Chamber with these notes too so that they could examine them, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to ask the Trial Chamber at the end. After the cross-examination, I was going to ask them to read out these notes so that you could hear them and the Trial Chamber, but it's no problem to photocopy them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will finish then.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would say for the record, though, it's my recollection the witness used the notes for one question to refresh his memory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was not going to raise the matter at all because to -- from what I could observe, and I do keep my eyes open, as you may have noticed to now, he was not referring to the notes. But he's volunteering these notes, and I have no problems if there is no problems forthcoming from your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just don't think that it's necessary for that there's any point, because he did not refer to those notes. He's referred from his own memory. He's referred from his -- he's used his recollection to give evidence. That's the evidence which is before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His expectation, Mr. Nicholls, is that he be given time to even make declarations based on those notes. So if we could avoid wasting time which is precious for Madam Richterova today, I would rather prefer proceeding the way I suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the meantime, unless you need them now, Mr. Biscevic, we can have them photocopied now so that you take the originals back with you when you leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are no problems, but I would just like to ask you: It's just two pages. Could I read it out in front of you? Could I read out what I think is the most important and then you can take it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your wish will be granted, but Mr. Nicholls. Please finish with your re-examination. We have five minutes. I really would like to finish with this witness within --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may help if I say why I'm here, because I think this may take some of the pressure off. I heard what was said earlier -- or I was sent an e-mail. Your Honour, it seems to me that there's only, at the moment, one realistic way of proceeding. I would ask Your Honour to sit all day tomorrow whatever hours it requires for this purpose. Ms. Richterova can deal with the witness. Both witnesses need to give evidence before Mr. McLeod, apparently, and I accept that. The -- I think we could start -- we will do Mr. McLeod certainly in chief. And I would ask that if we're sitting all day, whoever is cross-examining first cross-examines and then we'll see where we are at the end of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My position hasn't changed, Your Honour. I think we do Mr. McLeod on direct and cross-examination on Tuesday, and I still think that's a sensible suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not possible. That's why I said that. The reason is because there is still and will be still for part of Monday a witness part heard in the Stakic case. We're just having to proceed on the ordinary basis. There's no reason, in our submission, why the Defence, if there is time and the witness is finished in chief, should not begin cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you the reasons this morning, Your Honour, and I think they're valid. Materials were given us on Monday. There is not a B/C/S version of those materials yet in the hands on my client. I can't take instructions. I was going to meet with him Friday morning. I had scheduled a meeting between 10.00 and 12.00 Friday morning. That's now being taken away because Ms. Korner wants us to sit all day on Friday. And so the next opportunity I would have to meet with him would be on Monday. And that would mean that I couldn't possibly do my cross-examination until Tuesday. And if the witness has to stay here through Wednesday, that's -- that's just the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry that he has business problems, but he's here now under the control of the Trial Chamber and he should remain here until the Trial Chamber is satisfied --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, Ms. Korner, let's finish with this witness first, because I don't think it's proper that we discuss these things in his presence, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I -- Your Honour, I agree. But can I make it absolutely clear there is no question, as Mr. Ackerman says, of this witness being kept here on Wednesday. This witness has given up a lot of time to come and assist the Court. He has said that he has to be back for that and he won't be here, if that's what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If necessary, he will come again. I mean, it won't be the first time. But anyway, let's finish with this witness. Re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, Defence counsel for General Talic read out an additional part of the radio -- the tape-recording transcript and asked you whether or not you had read the portion attributed to you and you said that you did not. I'd like to read you the following section. This is on page 10 of the English translation. It begins at the top: "Female voice: We have received information on seized and returned weapons from Husmovci settlement. A successful operation by the 6th Krajina Brigade and the operative efforts of the Sanski Most public security station on 26, 27, and 28 May of this year have resulted in the seizure of illegally owned weapons and a large amount of ammunition," and it continues. Is that -- did you hear any broadcast of this type which referred specifically to the involvement of the 6th Krajina Brigade in disarming the population of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing in particular. No, I didn't hear it. They had their plan. For each particular area they would designate a military officer with a truck. A date and time would be given for collecting the weapons. And how it was actually done, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And very briefly when you refer to "they" in the answer you've just given, who are you speaking about? "They had their plan."

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th Krajina Brigade and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also questioned and asked about who was guarding you when you were in the MUP, and you confirmed that it was police. Just to clarify, did you not also say yesterday that soldiers in uniform would enter the MUP and beat you and other prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It was customary, because working hours were until 2.00 p.m. There was a joint building shared by the police and the army. Then the officer on duty who had the key, they would give the keys to the soldiers. They would unlock it and do what they wanted. That was a daily occurrence in the afternoons and the evenings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, counsel yesterday helped you refresh your recollection on some dates. And he showed you Prosecutor's Exhibit P608 and P609. Both of these -- P608 is an order signed by General Talic on the 1st of April, 1992. P609 is a regular combat report, signed on the 2nd of April, 1992. And both of those documents contain instructions for the 6th Krajina Brigade to go to Sanski Most and prevent inter-ethnic conflict. P608, the order, also states that the 6th Brigade is to establish full cooperation with the organs of government in Sanski Most municipality in collaboration with the TO and Territorial Defence units and the police. And that was used to show you that the arrival of Basara and the 6th Brigade would have been around the first week of April. At that time Mr. -- it was after that point, then, that Colonel Basara assured you as a representative of the Muslim community and the SDA that the army was there to guarantee peace and prevent war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then on the 19th of April - you were refreshed on that date or around that date - was the crisis at the municipality building when the non-Serbs were forced out. And you were asked questions about how the following day Mr. -- General Talic arrived by helicopter. And again you weren't at that meeting but you heard that he guaranteed peace and security and that there would not be war between different ethnic groups. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was like that. One thing was said and action was something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then about five weeks after that was the civilian order broadcast over the radio for people in your town, in your community, in Sanski Most, to turn over weapons. And those weapons were turned over to military officials at checkpoints; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Muslims and Croats. The Serbs didn't have that obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And on the 26th of May, shelling of Sanski Most began. Who was shelling Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army from the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They were shelling Muslim and Croat neighbourhoods only; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All Serbian houses are standing. The Muslim houses were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that Branko Basara did not keep his promise to the Muslim and Croat people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already stated that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Far from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But this has been brought up again. These statements have been shown. There's been the implication that there were these orders to prevent inter-ethnic conflict, and I think he should be given a full opportunity to explain what he thinks these orders were really about, these promises, what the motive for them was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said also that - I think it was on the first day - that when you first heard these guarantees from the JNA that you were -- and the Muslim and Croat people were happy because you thought there might be a chance that the army would fulfil its promise and prevent war between the different ethnicities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our only salvation. The Yugoslav People's Army should have been a guarantor of peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, as His Honour said yesterday, you're an educated man, you're a professional man. You were there, and you lived through all this. In your opinion, what was the purpose of these guarantees made to you by Branko Basara and General Talic that you could rely on them to protect you and prevent inter-ethnic conflict?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To mislead us so that they would be able to elaborate the plan they had in mind at peace. If -- but that is true. I would ask the Court once again as these are just two pages covering the chronology of events in the municipality of Sanski Most, that it should be read out so that we can see that there was a plan behind it with specific stages that followed one another in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. And I think he should be allowed to make a statement at the end if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Is there any objection on the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if -- if the witness is to use a certain -- certain notes concerning certain issues, then we are, of course, entitled to have that beforehand and cross-examine him on that. I don't really see any particular reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, he's making -- going to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Going to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He can make a statement but without consulting his notes. Because in that case, we will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But if he has a pre-prepared statement, which he wants to read, I see no problem in -- in not -- allowing to do so. And then obviously we'll have -- he will make it now, and if you have any questions you would like to ask afterwards, I will give you the opportunity. Go ahead, please. Go ahead. You can read out this statement or make your statement. Please be as short as you can. Thank you. And we'll have the break immediately after.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chronology of events in Sana. On the 14th of March 1992, the 6th Krajina Brigade arrived with Basara Brana as commander. On the 14th of April, 1992 the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most was proclaimed and a Crisis Staff was formed. For control in the Crisis Staff, Rasula Nedeljko, Vrkes Vlado, Vrucinic Mirko, Basara Branko, Anicic Nedeljko, Lukic Slobodan, Savanovic Boro, Banjac Bosko, Tadic Boro, Tripkovic Nemanja, Davidovic Nenad, Ergarac Dane, Jaglica Nebojsa, Delic Tomo, Krunic Mico and others were appointed. On the 17th of April, 1992 workers, Muslims and Croats, were chased out of the MUP. Nedeljko Rasula was in charge of this action. On the 19th of April, the Crisis Staff was formed consisting of SOS, SDS, and the 6th Krajina Brigade of Basara's -- no. Basara commanded this operation of formation of this staff. That is when executives, Muslims and Catholics, were chased out of the social accounting service, the court, the prosecutor's office, the radio station, the public utility company, Famos, the hospital, educational institutions, and the municipal assembly. On the 15th of May, 1992 all employed were fired, a curfew was introduced, patrols by the military police and the 6th Krajina Brigade, instruction at school was suspended.
